summary: This specification defines the JSON merge patch format and processing rules, mainly meant for the HTTP PATCH method to describe changes to a target resource. It was replaced by RFC 7396.

eli5.summary: Instead of sending an entire form again, send only the parts that changed. This RFC describes a simple way to do that for JSON data. It was replaced by a newer version.

questions: how do you use merge patch with http
why was json merge patch replaced
subtitle: A simple way to describe updates to JSON data by sending only the parts that changed.

tldr.problem: When updating a JSON resource via HTTP, sending the entire updated document is wasteful. A patch format should let you send only the changes.
tldr.mechanism: JSON merge patch uses a document that mirrors the structure of the target, with new and modified values included literally and null values marking deletions.
tldr.outcome: This simple format became popular for HTTP PATCH, but was later superseded by RFC 7396 (JSON Patch), which is more powerful for array operations.

today: RFC 7386 is a Standards Track document from October 2014, but it has been obsoleted by RFC 7396 (JSON Patch), which provides a more complete patch format suitable for arrays and other use cases.

sections.title: A Simple Patch Format for JSON
sections.content:
RFC 7386 defines the JSON merge patch format, a way to describe a set of modifications to a JSON document using a syntax that mimics the document being modified. The merge patch is intended primarily for use with the HTTP PATCH method to update a resource.

The core idea is intuitive: to describe changes, send a document that shows what the target should look like after the patch, but only for the parts you want to change. Recipients compare the patch against the current content to determine the exact changes.
sections.eli5: To change something in JSON, describe it the way you want it to look after the change. The server figures out what to do by comparing your description to what it already has.

sections.title: How Merge Patch Works
sections.content:
The merge patch process follows a simple recursive algorithm. When the patch is an object, each member name either adds a new key-value pair to the target or replaces an existing one. The key difference from a naive replacement is the treatment of null values: a null value in the patch means delete that key from the target.

If the patch is not an object (for instance, a string or array), the entire target is replaced with the entire patch. This means arrays are replaced wholesale, not updated element-by-element. This limitation is one reason RFC 7396 was later created.
sections.eli5: If you set something to null, it gets deleted. Otherwise, the new value overwrites the old one. If you send something that is not an object shape, it replaces everything.

sections.title: A Concrete Example
sections.content:
Given a JSON document with a title, author object, tags array, and content, a client can send a patch that changes the title from "Goodbye!" to "Hello!", adds a new phoneNumber field, removes the familyName from the author, and replaces the entire tags array. A single PATCH request with the merge patch applied produces the modified document.

The resulting document contains all the original fields except for the deleted familyName (set to null in the patch), and includes the new phoneNumber field. The tags array and author's givenName remain or are updated as specified. The content field is untouched because it did not appear in the patch.
sections.eli5: You send the server your changes as a JSON object. It compares it with what it has, applies adds and updates, and deletes anything you set to null.

sections.title: The MIME Type and Processing Rules
sections.content:
RFC 7386 registers the MIME media type application/merge-patch+json for this format. The media type indicates that the body conforms to both JSON and the merge patch processing rules.

Merge patch documents operate at the data level, not the textual level. The processing does not preserve whitespace, member ordering, number precision beyond the target implementation's capabilities, or other textual features. If the target implementation allows duplicate names (which is not valid JSON), the result is undefined.
sections.eli5: Servers use the label application/merge-patch+json to know how to handle the patch. The exact text formatting does not matter; only the data structure counts.

sections.title: Security and Applicability
sections.content:
The merge patch format is unsuitable for JSON structures that rely on explicit null values or that use arrays as data containers requiring element-level updates. The RFC acknowledges this limitation: merge patch is designed for object-centric JSON and assumes null values are not meaningful data.

Security considerations are inherited from RFC 5789 (the HTTP PATCH method). The server, not the client, bears responsibility for determining the appropriateness of changes and verifying authorization. The merge patch format itself does not add new security concerns beyond those of JSON and HTTP PATCH.
sections.eli5: This format works best for object-based data where null means delete. If you need to update arrays item-by-item, or if your data uses null as a real value, a different patch format is better.
